title: Tumefactive demyelination after covid-19 successfully treated with betainterferon 1A
case_prompt: A 20-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with 4 days of left lower-limb paresthesia that progressed to weakness and visual blurring. She reported no fever, dysphagia, or sphincter disturbances. On examination, she had complete, proportionate left hemiparesis with pyramidal signs and clonus, reduced proprioception and vibration in the lower limbs, and tactile and painful hypoesthesia on the left side. Ocular movement demonstrated impaired smooth pursuit on right gaze, speech was mildly scanning, and gait was hemiparetic. Laboratory testing—including infectious, inflammatory, and rheumatologic panels—was negative. Brain MRI revealed diffuse T2/FLAIR hyperintense and T1 hypointense subcortical lesions involving the periventricular white matter and brainstem. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed mild pleocytosis and elevated protein. She received a 5-day course of intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day) with partial improvement and was discharged for outpatient follow-up.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious, inflammatory, and rheumatologic disorders considered and excluded — “The differential diagnosis was made with infectious, inflammatory, and rheumatologic tests and all of them were negative.”  
2. Tumefactive demyelination considered based on enlarging lesions with heterogeneous enhancement — “At that moment, the main differential diagnosis was tumecfative demyelination…”  
3. Neoplasm (brain tumor) considered due to progressive lesions and enhancement pattern — “…or tumor.”  
4. Typical multiple sclerosis considered less likely given the fast and aggressive presentation, neurological deterioration, and failure of initial therapy — “Due to the fast and aggressive presentation with neurological deterioration and failure of initial therapy, the possibility of Marburg's variant of MS was suggested.”
